title: Gray hair isn't wisdom (256–262)
hookLine: one is not learned because he talks much, nor an elder because his hair is gray
carry: wisdom can live in any body

lines: THE ONE WHO TALKS THE MOST.
THE ONE WHO'S BEEN AROUND LONGEST.
cards: Every office has one: the person who talks the most in meetings, so everyone assumes they know the most. Every family has one too: the relative who reminds you they've been around longer, so they must be right.

And sometimes it's the quiet twenty-five-year-old in the corner who actually understands the problem, or the grandmother who says almost nothing and sees everything. Loud isn't learned. Old isn't wise.
Easy to say, and easy to forget in the moment. Chapter nineteen of the Dhammapada sorts the real thing from the look of it.

teach.h: LABELS AND WHAT THEY STAND FOR.
teach.b: The chapter is called Dhammaṭṭhavagga, the chapter of the one who stands in the dhamma, and it pulls apart labels and the qualities they're supposed to stand for. A judge isn't just because he forces a decision.

Verse two fifty-eight, in Max Müller's words: "A man is not learned because he talks much; he who is patient, free from hatred and fear, he is called learned." Learning shows up as patience and fearlessness, not volume.
Then verse two sixty: "A man is not an elder because his head is grey".

The Pali word for elder is thera, the same word in Theravāda, the way of the elders. And the verse has a sharp name for someone merely old: moghajiṇṇa, in Müller's English, old-in-vain. Aged, but for nothing.
So what makes a real elder? Verse two sixty-one: "He in whom there is truth, virtue, love, restraint, moderation, he who is free from impurity and is wise, he is called an elder."
The commentary tells a story that turns it around.

teach.h: THE SMALL MONK WAS THE ELDER.
teach.b: A group of monks came to visit the Buddha, and on their way in they passed a small, youthful-looking monk named Bhaddiya, who was just leaving. The Buddha asked if they'd seen the elder who had just gone out.
They said they'd only seen a young novice. The Buddha told them the one they passed was an elder indeed, awakened. It wasn't his age that made him one.
Wisdom can live in any body, at any age. So can its absence.

how: In Theravada monasteries seniority is counted by rains retreats since ordination, and senior monks are called thera; these verses remind the community that the title means little without the qualities behind it.

o: an elder, made one by virtue, not by age
a monk who has lived past seventy years
a teacher who gives the longest sermons

games.q: match each label to what it really takes.
p: patient, free from hatred and fear

s: verse 258 says the one who talks most is most learned
"a man is not learned because he talks much."
thera, elder, is the same word as in Theravāda
Theravāda: the way of the elders.
in the commentary, the visiting monks recognized Bhaddiya as an elder
they took him for a young novice; the Buddha told them he was an elder, awakened.

games.q: you're one of the visiting monks. on your way in, you pass a small, young-looking monk who is just leaving. the Buddha asks: did you see the elder who just left? what do you say?
games.why: they saw only a novice. the Buddha said that was Bhaddiya, a true elder: age and size had nothing to do with it.

practice: Think of one person who has really taught you something, not by talking a lot but by who they are, older or younger than you, and picture what they had: patience, honesty, restraint. If gratitude comes, let it stay a moment.
Then ask quietly which of those qualities you could grow without announcing it, something to earn slowly, not claim, and let the question rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Thera. An elder: verse two sixty says one isn't an elder because the head is gray; truth, virtue, kindness and restraint make an elder.

orig.note: Pali: an elder — the word in Theravāda, the way of the elders; verse 260 says gray hair alone doesn't make one.

carryVoice: Your line: wisdom can live in any body. Gray hair or not. See you tomorrow.
